name: Rap Lore
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Montserrat SemiBold with picked words in Montserrat Bold, on an
orange card, in three colours offered for the type and the same three
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.

the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.

_comment_face: Montserrat SemiBold. Which cut that is, why the full name rather
than 'Montserrat' is declared, and what the machine may already
know it by are written out in
It is the lightest face any pack under this heading sets a block
in apart from Hall of Femme's hairline, and it is legible at that
weight for Hall of Femme's reason: the type is not over the
photograph at all, it is on a card in a colour somebody chose. A
600-weight geometric sans over an unknown still would be a risk
taken forty times a run; on the card it is a choice.
expulsion-science is the other pack set in this family, and the
two are worth reading together: it takes the Bold and the
ExtraBold, this one takes the SemiBold and the Bold. The same
100-unit step, one cut lower - which is the family's own idea of
emphasis used twice rather than a weight picked for this show.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the three in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is
found by matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the orange card is the pairing this show opens
on, and it is the brand pairing rather than the strongest one in
the palette. Worth stating plainly, because it is the one number
here somebody may check: white on #FF7300 is 2.7 to 1, just under
the 3:1 the large-text threshold asks for, while black on the same
card is 7.7 to 1. The orange is a light colour and the neutral
that reads best against it is the dark one - the other way round
from the pink- and red-carded packs under this heading, where the
card is dark and the white is the safe neutral.
It is left as the default all the same, and the reason is what
these numbers describe. The threshold is written for body text
read at length; this is a 600-weight sans set at the preset's 40px
on a 540-wide frame - capitals about a twelfth of the frame high -
with a card of solid colour behind it and nothing else on it. And
black is one press away in the same row, which is what the palette
is for: a user who finds a still where the white does not hold has
the stronger pairing beside it rather than a support request.
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - three buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same three in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does and for their reason: the point
is the PAIRING. Nine combinations of a white, a black and the
brand orange, and the ones worth having are the ones that read. A
palette that could only ever be used one way round would be a
palette of three cards, and this show's look is the pairing rather
than any one of them.
Three where its neighbours offer four, because the show has three
colours. The lists are as long as a pack wants them - the row
draws a swatch per entry and wraps - so a palette is the brand's
colours and not a fixed-size control to be padded out to match the
pack next door.
The absolute white and the absolute black are meant as written:
#FFFFFF and #000000, not an off-white or a soft black. On a card
of one saturated colour the neutrals are what carry the contrast,
and a neutral pulled towards the card spends contrast to buy a
softness nobody asked for at this size.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the two
neutrals, then the brand colour - and the two defaults are picked
out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens on the
first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom Hall of
Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one order.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white or black on black.
That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent because
the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the three matching
combinations would cost the panel more explaining than an
invisible caption costs a user, who can see it is invisible and
presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Montserrat Bold, in the same colour as the
rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and expulsion-science's both.
600 to 700 is one step of the family and it is a quiet highlight -
quieter than Hall of Femme's, which puts 200 against 800 and is as
loud as a box would be. That is the step this family has at this
end of its range, and the alternative is not a louder step but a
different kind of emphasis: the ExtraBold is two steps away and
would pick words out of a 600 block hard enough to read as a
second face rather than as a stress. A caption is one sentence
long and the picked word sits inside it, so the stress is the
right size of gesture and the card stays one clean shape.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Orange, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching
this value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be
written in the order the show states its colours in while the
channel still opens on white type and an orange card.
#FF7300 is the only card under this heading that is not a pink, a
magenta, a red or a champagne, and that is what makes this show
itself at a glance: the card is the shape that is a fifth of the
frame and reads before anything on it, so it is what carries the
colour, and the type is what has to stay legible against it. It is
also the lightest card of any of them, which is why the note on
`color` above spends a paragraph on which neutral holds against it
- on this card that question has the opposite answer to its

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
